label: Getting started with Model-as-a-Service on Fusion
description: Deploy the full MaaS platform on IBM Fusion HCI with GitOps: install OpenShift AI operators, connect Fusion object storage, stand up a Model Registry, deploy GPU-backed inference, expose models through an API gateway, and validate a live endpoint.

label: Configure subscription-based model governance on Fusion MaaS
description: Put access control and quota management in place for your running models: deploy MaaSSubscription and MaaSAuthPolicy resources with the maas-config Helm chart via ArgoCD, create API keys, and enforce per-group token rate limits through the gateway.

label: CPU-based LLM inference on Fusion with GitOps
description: Deploy small open-source language models (Qwen2.5, SmolLM2) on standard x86 CPU nodes using the vLLM CPU ServingRuntime for KServe — no GPU required. All resources are declared in Git and reconciled by ArgoCD on IBM Fusion.

label: Build an agentic chat assistant on Fusion AI
description: Deploy a production-ready React + FastAPI chat application on IBM Fusion using ArgoCD, HashiCorp Vault, External Secrets Operator, and Stakater Reloader — with automated secret rotation, unified model selection across gateway and KServe, and RAG-powered responses via CAS.

label: Registering models from the Model Catalog
description: Import and register foundation models from HuggingFace or the Red Hat model repository into the Model Registry, including versioning and metadata setup, before you deploy them for inference.

label: Getting started with Namespace-as-a-Service on Fusion
description: Turn namespace provisioning into a self-service Developer Hub wizard backed by GitOps: platform-team setup, GitHub auth, Helm values, the ArgoCD controller, and the developer flow for requesting, resizing, and deleting namespaces with auto-applied RBAC and quotas.

label: Building agents with the watsonx Orchestrate AI Builder
description: Describe the agent you want and let the AI Builder generate it from scratch, then refine it through conversation or by feeding back past interactions to adjust its behavior.

label: Running watsonx Orchestrate Developer Edition locally
description: Set up the local watsonx Orchestrate server and UI on your own machine, giving you a dedicated environment with its own API endpoints to build and test agents.

label: Creating and building AI agents with the watsonx Orchestrate ADK
description: Install the watsonx Orchestrate Agent Development Kit and build agents using either the conversational AI Builder or declarative YAML definitions, including tools, connections, and knowledge bases.

label: Deploying agents in watsonx Orchestrate
description: Release a working agent into production so users can access it, either through the watsonx Orchestrate UI or the ADK command-line interface, and undeploy it when it's no longer needed.

label: Deploying watsonx.ai and watsonx Orchestrate on Fusion HCI
description: Use the Software Hub service on IBM Fusion HCI to automate prerequisites, storage class selection, and resource pre-checks before installing watsonx.ai and watsonx Orchestrate.

label: AI workloads on IBM Fusion HCI
description: How IBM Fusion HCI runs container and VM AI workloads on its GPU nodes, validated end-to-end with watsonx for consistent training and inference performance.

label: GPU servers and sizing on Fusion HCI
description: Reference for available GPU server hardware, card counts, and capacity on Fusion HCI, used to size GPU nodes for Model-as-a-Service inference workloads.

label: Getting started with Fusion Developer Hub
description: Deploy Red Hat Developer Hub on Fusion using GitOps, the platform both NaaS and MaaS self-service templates run on top of.

label: Getting started with Fusion GitOps (ArgoCD)
description: Install OpenShift GitOps and ArgoCD on your Fusion cluster, the reconciliation engine the NaaS controller and other self-service templates depend on.

label: Understanding IBM Fusion's AI Data Platform for inference
description: Learn why unified namespace, AFM data federation, and CAS auto-refreshed embeddings matter for AI inference cost and quality, and how to size NVMe working sets versus federated capacity storage to cut token economics.
